title: Alcaraz Loses at 3:34 A.M., Walks Off Smiling: 'I Suffered, But I Enjoyed'
summary:
Most tennis players would not smile after losing a five-set match at 3:34 in the morning. Carlos Alcaraz is not most players.

After his US Open title defense ended against Ben Shelton — a grueling four-hour, 28-minute battle — the 23-year-old Spaniard was filmed walking down the Arthur Ashe tunnel with a huge grin. It was the latest finish in the tournament's history.

Why the smile? Alcaraz had been out for over five months with a wrist injury that left him in pain every day. He missed the French Open and Wimbledon. He didn't know if he'd even play in New York until a week before.

"I suffered, but I enjoyed and that's why I smiled when I walked out of the court because I missed that feeling," he said.

The late finish wasn't unusual at this US Open. Eventual champion Alexander Zverev finished past 1 a.m. in three of his first five matches. Venus Williams finished her first-round match at 2 a.m.

"I think it's too much," Alcaraz said of the schedule. "The last match people stayed but if that match was played earlier, the court could have been packed." He suggested a maximum finish time of 11 p.m.

Alcaraz isn't the only player who missed big chunks of the season. Britain's Jack Draper struggled with an arm injury and ended his season early. Alcaraz's rival Jannik Sinner missed the US Open with a knee injury. Alcaraz said he'll skip some tournaments in the future to stay "mentally and physically healthy."

This week, he's competing for Team Europe in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London, captained by Yannick Noah against a World team led by Andre Agassi.

"When you have your team-mates, the best in the world, by your side, it's a weird feeling but it's beautiful," he said. "We played like our lives depend on it."
why_it_matters: Elite sport's calendar and workload have become a health issue: when star players openly choose rest over prize money and tournaments run past 3 a.m., the sport faces pressure to redesign schedules around the athletes, not only around television audiences.

background_read: The US Open is one of tennis's four Grand Slam tournaments — the biggest events of the year — played on hard courts in New York at the end of the summer. Its main court, Arthur Ashe Stadium, is the largest tennis arena in the world and is named after Arthur Ashe (the first Black man to win a Grand Slam singles title).
Unlike the other Slams, the US Open puts on night sessions that can run past midnight, and players have complained about the late finishes for years.

Carlos Alcaraz (a Spanish player born in 2003) became world No. 1 and a Grand Slam champion while still a teenager, and his matches against Italy's Jannik Sinner are seen as the sport's new great rivalry. The Laver Cup (a team event started in 2017 in which Team Europe plays a "World" team) is named after Rod Laver, an Australian often called one of the greatest players ever. Yannick Noah is a former French Open champion, and Andre Agassi, who leads the World team, is an American who won eight Grand Slam singles titles.

perspectives.perspective: Fans who stayed to watch the marathon
perspectives.description: For them the finish was unforgettable drama: two players trading shots in an empty, floodlit stadium at dawn. Alcaraz smiling through a defeat gave the loss a strange, likable dignity that a trophy lift could not.

They see a clear warning sign. Bodies cannot recover from four-and-a-half-hour matches played after midnight, and the injury list across the tour — wrists, arms, knees — suggests the schedule, not just bad luck, is the problem.

Night sessions exist because they sell tickets and attract prime-time television money, and evenings in New York are when the biggest audiences tune in. An 11 p.m. finish cap would be expensive for them, which is why the debate has lasted so long.

perspectives.perspective: Alcaraz and his team looking ahead
perspectives.description: He has already said he will skip tournaments to stay mentally and physically healthy, a choice that could cost ranking points and prize money. Whether that becomes normal for the next generation of stars will shape how tennis is played.
